teaser: Barefoot, in a dress as light as a nightgown: the most admired woman in Paris, just as she wished.
review_notes:
Dimensions given as about 225 x 148 cm.
City of Paris purchase dated 1860: please confirm against the Carnavalet record.
Portrait given to Prince Augustus of Prussia and returned to Juliette after his death in 1843 under his will: standard account, worth a check.
The dark rippled surface behind the footstool is read as water (tour spot 'Bare feet'); worded cautiously.
'Said to have refused a place at Napoleon's court' is the traditional account.
Juliette's failing eyesight in the 1840s (cataracts) is from biographies.

lesson.text: This canvas is 2.25 meters tall, about 7 feet 5 inches. Stand in front of it at the Musée Carnavalet in Paris and the young woman on the chair is as large as you are, seated at your level, close enough to speak to. That scale was usually kept for kings and generals. Here it goes to a banker's wife in her twenties.

Her name was Juliette Récamier, and around 1800 she was the most talked-about woman in Paris. Writers, politicians and generals crowded her salon, a regular gathering in a private home where guests came to talk. She was known for her beauty, her white dresses and a gift for making each visitor feel like the favorite.
Juliette was married at 15 to Jacques Récamier, a rich banker more than twenty-five years older than she was. The wedding took place in 1793, in the most violent months of the French Revolution.

François Gérard was not her first choice. In 1800 she posed for Jacques-Louis David, the most powerful painter in France. He worked slowly, she grew impatient, and she turned to his former pupil. David never finished his version. It hangs in the Louvre today, bare background and all, and shows her reclining on a sofa, cool and far away.
Gérard gave her what David had not: warmth. Follow how he does it, from her face down to the floor.

lesson.title: From curls to toes
lesson.text: She sits sideways on an antique-style chair, turned toward you. Four stops, top to bottom.

spots.title: The tilt
spots.text: Her head leans toward one shoulder and her eyes meet yours with a half smile. Dark curls are pinned up loosely. Nothing here is stiff: she looks as if you have just walked in.

spots.title: The dress
spots.text: White, gathered just under the bust, slipping off one shoulder, with a small ruffle at the neckline. This light cotton gown was the fashion of the day, and a daring one: nothing structured underneath.

spots.title: The shawl
spots.text: A wide golden-yellow shawl slides off her lap and pools on the floor, its patterned border hanging down at the left. Shawls of fine wool from Kashmir were the luxury item of the moment.

spots.title: Bare feet
spots.text: No shoes, no stockings. One foot rests on a low wooden stool, the other on cool marble. Just behind the stool, the dark surface with pale ripples appears to be water.

lesson.text: Bare feet in a full-length portrait: twenty years earlier that would have been unthinkable for a respectable woman. But after the Revolution, Paris dreamed of ancient Greece and Rome. Women gave up corsets and wide skirts for simple white tunics copied from marble statues. Juliette dresses like a statue and smiles like a neighbor.
Neoclassicism, the taste for the clean lines of ancient Greece and Rome, is often called cold. Gérard shows it can be tender: antique columns and costume, with a living person in the middle of them.

Now the room. It is less a room than a stage set: a stone porch open to a garden, heavy columns, an arch. Gérard has hung a red cloth behind her head, the way a photographer hangs a backdrop. Everything hard and upright is arranged so that one soft, slanting body stands out.
Three lines show how the picture is built.

lines.label: The column
lines.text: A thick column runs most of the height on the right. Straight, dark and cold: everything she is not.

lines.label: The arch
lines.text: Above her, a round arch opens onto trees, sky and a pale building. It repeats, much larger, the rounded shapes of her head and shoulders.

lines.label: Her body
lines.text: Her pose draws one long slanting curve from the curls to the toes, crossing most of the canvas. Against so many verticals, the eye cannot miss it.

lesson.text: Gérard knew how to flatter without lying. Born in Rome to a French father and an Italian mother, trained in David's studio, he became the portraitist everyone in power wanted. He painted Napoleon's family, then the kings who returned after Napoleon. Changing regimes did his career no harm at all.
Gérard's success earned him a nickname that sounds like a tongue twister: “the painter of kings and the king of painters.”

For Juliette, fame had a price. Her salon welcomed people who disliked Napoleon, and she is said to have refused a place at his court. In 1811, after she visited her friend Madame de Staël, a writer he had already banished, he ordered Juliette to keep away from Paris too. She came back only after his fall.
In French, a “récamier” is a daybed with raised ends and no back. The piece of furniture is named after Juliette, thanks to the sofa she lies on in David's unfinished portrait.

And this portrait? She gave it away. In 1807 Prince Augustus of Prussia fell in love with her and hoped to marry her. She stayed with her husband and sent the prince the painting instead. It hung in his palace in Berlin for decades, and his will ordered that it go back to her.

He died in 1843, and the canvas came home to Paris. Juliette was 65 by then, and her eyesight was failing. The woman on the chair was still in her twenties, still smiling at whoever walked in. Juliette died in 1849, and the city of Paris bought the portrait in 1860.

quiz.question: Why did Juliette Récamier turn to Gérard for her portrait?
options: David worked slowly and she lost patience
quiz.explanation: She had posed for David in 1800, but he was slow and never finished his version.

quiz.question: What inspired the simple white dress and bare feet?
options: Court dress under the old kings
quiz.explanation: After the Revolution, fashion copied the plain tunics seen on antique marble statues.

quiz.question: What is a “récamier” in French today?
quiz.explanation: The daybed takes its name from the sofa in David's portrait of her.

quiz.question: To whom did Juliette give Gérard's portrait?
quiz.explanation: The Prussian prince wanted to marry her; she sent him the painting instead.

quiz.question: In the picture, what does the long slanting line of her body play against?
options: Straight verticals such as the column
quiz.explanation: Columns and other upright forms make her soft diagonal pose stand out.

facts.text: Gérard's portrait shows Juliette Récamier about life-size.
facts.explanation: The canvas is 2.25 meters tall, so the seated figure is as large as a real person.

facts.text: David completed his portrait of Juliette before Gérard began his.
facts.explanation: David never finished his version; it hangs unfinished in the Louvre.

facts.text: Napoleon ordered Juliette Récamier to stay away from Paris.
facts.explanation: In 1811, after she visited the banished Madame de Staël, he exiled her from the capital.
